pullQuote.title: As good as gold
pullQuote.quote: Very good club. Performs as well as my Vokey SM10, and Cleveland RTX wedges. Consistent distances and puts good spin on the ball. All around solid performer.

buyBody: Everything inside a hundred yards gets easier. The Carver comes off the face soft, grabs the ball hard enough to stop it near where you aimed, and tells you honestly when you didn't. Six lofts, right and left hand, sixty days to decide whether it stays in the bag.

four.v: Send it back if it isn't the one

whatYouGet: One Carver 01 Gold wedge in the loft and hand you picked
Lucky Golf stock steel shaft (KBS becomes an option soon)
No headcover — none of our clubs ship with one
carePara: The gold finish is a finish, not a coating you have to baby, but grooves full of sand don't spin anything. Brush the face after a round and dry the head before it goes back in the bag.
A headcover is worth it if your clubs rattle around in the cart. Several reviewers mention picking up cart rash without one.
marquee: Six lofts, right and left hand
Sold direct, never through a middleman
clubHeadline: The kind of wedge that makes a short-sided miss feel survivable.
clubParas: Pick it up and it feels like a club that costs more. That's the forging — 1020 soft carbon steel rather than cast, which is what gives you the soft strike and the honest feedback when you catch one thin.

The face is where the work happens. CNC-milled grooves with micro-milling in the land between them, over a sandblasted finish, so there's texture on the ball across the whole face and not just in the grooves. That's what produces the check-up and the one-hop stop, and it's what keeps working out of wet grass.
Weighting shifts as the loft goes up. The higher lofts run toe-weighted for finesse around the green; the lower ones sit with a lower center of gravity for cleaner full swings. Same club, six jobs.

clubSpecs.v: Forged players' wedge, full six-loft lineup.
Soft. 1020 carbon steel reports back on every strike, good and bad.
CNC-milled grooves, micro-milled between, over a sandblasted finish.
Shifts by loft — toe-weighted high for finesse, lower CG low for full swings.
Anyone replacing a stock wedge that has stopped gripping the ball.

helpLoft.headline: Start with the wedge you already carry
helpLoft.sub: Wedges work in gaps. Four to six degrees between clubs keeps your distances even and stops two wedges going the same yardage. Tell us the loft of your pitching wedge and we'll do the arithmetic.

specSub: One head, two soles and six lofts. Everything below is the manufacturer's sheet; where the K and the S differ, both are listed.

specTabs.aside: Both grinds are the same forged 1020 head at 300 g. Where they differ is the sole, and the bounce and lie that come with it. The S measures more bounce than the K at the same loft and plays less of it, because the narrower sole puts less of itself on the turf.

look.photo: Bold, full-bleed, portrait. The gold head caught in low sun as it comes out of the bag on the tee box — other players in soft focus behind. This is the hero of the section; it should stop the scroll on its own.
look.headline: You'll want to pull it out of the bag
paras: Most wedges are gray. This one isn't, and you find out what that's worth the first time you take it out on a busy tee box. People ask. They always ask.

That's not the reason to buy it — the face is. But it isn't nothing, either. Golf is a game you play for four hours with the same three people, and the club you look down at should be one you actually like looking at.
look.aside: Everyone else is carrying the same club with someone else's name on it. It's better to be lucky.

quote.q: I have played 10 plus rounds with this club and I love it. I can confidently place the ball within 5ft of where I am aiming with this thing.
quote.name: Dan T.

jmSummary.text: Customers praised this premium forged wedge for its “crazy spin and control” and eye-catching gold finish. Many said it performs “as well as big name brands” at a better price. The club features CNC-milled grooves, soft feel, and solid construction. However, one customer reported the head separating from shaft on first swing, and another noted slow customer service response times.

closeBody: The Carver is $99 in every loft, right hand or left. Sixty days to send it back if it isn't the one.

GRIND COPY — sourced, no longer a draft.
1. SOURCE IS THE SPEC-TO-BENEFIT TRANSLATION GUIDE v1.0 (Cole supplied it 2026-08-01, references-spec-to-benefit-v1.0.md). It defines both grinds directly: K is "a wider, flatter sole profile with a standard leading edge... the no-surprises wedge... built for the golfer who strikes cleanly and plays primarily from standard lies"; S is "a narrower, more relieved sole with a reshaped leading edge... the versatility wedge... tight lies, awkward angles, open-face lobs".
2. THIS REVERSES AN EARLIER CORRECTION. HANDOFF §24d recorded that the S is NOT the open-face versatility grind, on the basis that our letters are Vokey's and that is Vokey's M. Lucky's own written guide says otherwise, and a company document about what Lucky's specs mean outranks an inference from another maker's nomenclature. The site now follows the guide. If Cole wants the Vokey reading back, this is the block to change.
3. IT ALSO CLOSES §24a's open question. "Is our S actually narrower, does it have a tapered rear sole" is answered in writing: narrower, more relieved, reshaped leading edge. This block is no longer the unverified one.
4. Every number in `facts` is still the manufacturer sheet, and the measured-vs-effective bounce note still stands — a narrow relieved sole carrying more measured bounce than a wide flat one is exactly what the geometry predicts.

grinds.headline: Same head. Two soles.
grinds.sub: Grind is the shape of the sole — the part of the club that meets the turf. It is the only thing that changes between a 01 in K and a 01 in S: same forged 1020 head, same 300 g, same milled and sandblasted face, same price.

options.name: The no-surprises one
options.forWho: Standard lies, and a square setup
paras: K grind is the wider, flatter sole, with a standard leading edge. Spreading turf contact over more of the sole is what stops the club digging, so it bottoms out in the same place shot after shot — set up square, swing through, take your divot, and it does what you expect.

That makes it the one for standard lies: fairway, rough, fringe, full swings and the straightforward short-game shots. The bounce steps with the loft rather than sitting flat — 8° on the 50 and the 52, where you are hitting full shots and do not want the sole in the way; 12° on the 54 and the 56, which are the ones you take into a bunker; 10° on the 58 and the 60.

facts.v: Wider and flatter, standard leading edge
8° at 50 and 52 · 12° at 54 and 56 · 10° at 58 and 60

options.name: The versatile one
options.forWho: Tight lies, and an open face
paras: S grind takes relief off the heel and the trailing edge and reshapes the leading edge, so there is less sole meeting the ground. Open the face and the club still sits low behind the ball instead of riding up on its own bounce.

That is what makes it the versatile one. Off a tight lie the reshaped leading edge slides under the ball where a wider sole would skip into it, and out of a bunker or off an awkward angle you can work the face without the club fighting you. More shots, from more places.

facts.v: Narrower and relieved, reshaped leading edge

grinds.measured: Bounce on a spec sheet is measured off the sole, and it is not the whole story. A wide, flat sole puts more of itself on the ground, so it plays every degree it measures. A narrower sole with the heel and the trailing edge ground away presents less — which is why the S reads higher on paper than the K at the same loft and still slides rather than bounces off a tight lie. The numbers below are real; read them alongside the sole, not instead of it.
grinds.short: Short version: K for standard lies and a square setup, S for tight lies and an open face.
grinds.note: Bounce, loft and lie are the manufacturer's published figures and the full table by loft is further down this page. The sole descriptions are the standard meaning of a K and an S grind.
